name: Temple fade

card.summary: A temple fade is a haircut that tapers the hair short at the temples, sharpening the hairline and framing the face.
card.note: Barber service; grows out within weeks.

quick.overview:
A temple fade is a barber technique in which the hair around the temples is clipped short and blended into the longer hair above, giving a clean, defined edge around the hairline.
People use it to frame the forehead, tidy the sides, and make a hairline appear sharper, often under a textured top or a longer style.
quick.how: A barber uses clippers with different guard lengths and blades to taper the hair in the temple area, then outlines the edge. Many people refresh it every few weeks as hair grows back.
quick.risks: Hair clippers and razors can cause irritation or razor bumps in some people. A very short temple area also reveals a receding hairline.

lead: A temple fade, also called a temp fade, is a fade or taper concentrated at the temples. In barbering a fade means the hair is cut with clippers that arc out of the hair so the lengths blend seamlessly from short to longer [1].

Looksmaxxing and grooming discussions treat the cut as a way to clean up the hairline and frame the face. Wikipedia's article on the regular haircut covers tapers and fades but does not describe the temple fade specifically, listing it only as a related cut [1].
No clinical research exists on this haircut.

chain: Hair at the temples is tapered short
Hairline edge looks cleaner and more defined
Face appears more framed and groomed
angle.text: The temple fade changes the outline around the forehead and sides, which is why it is used to neaten the hairline and add contrast with the hair on top.

infobox: Regular barber visits as hair grows

paras: Fades are cut with taper or fade clippers, whose lever or fine-blade range lets the barber gradually change cutting length. Edgers with very fine blades outline around the ears and nape, and shears over comb are used for blending [1]. Guards are numbered in eighths of an inch, so a #1 guard leaves about an eighth of an inch of hair [1].

Short-back-and-sides cuts date back to Roman legionaries and returned in the Renaissance and Regency era, and tapered cuts became the norm for professional men by about 1910 [1]. The undercut was adopted in hipster culture in the 2010s [1].
